title: HGS and Shielded VMs in Plain English
summary: Understand why Host Guardian Service exists, what it trusts, and how it protects shielded VM startup from an untrusted or compromised fabric.
plain_language_explanation: A guarded fabric separates the people who operate Hyper-V from the authority that decides whether a host is trusted enough to receive the keys needed to start a shielded VM. HGS performs attestation and key protection. A healthy Hyper-V host alone is not sufficient: the host must satisfy the configured HGS trust policy before protected keys are released.
quick_check: Why is HGS more than just another highly available Windows service?

title: Guarded Fabric Architecture, HGS Trust Boundary and Separation of Duties
summary: Design HGS as a security authority with explicit administrative, directory, certificate and availability boundaries rather than as an ordinary Hyper-V management component.
objective: Explain HGS attestation, key protection, administrative separation, cluster availability and why the HGS trust boundary must be designed independently from the fabric it protects.
body_outline: A guarded fabric combines HGS, guarded Hyper-V hosts and shielded VMs; HGS attests hosts and releases protected keys only to trusted hosts.
HGS is commonly deployed as a three-node cluster so loss of one node does not remove the trust authority required by shielded workloads.
HGS administrators should be separated from fabric administrators wherever practical because control of both sides weakens the protection against malicious or compromised administrators.
The HGS directory/forest, signing and encryption certificates, DNS reachability and service availability are security dependencies, not merely infrastructure details.
HGS disaster recovery must preserve attestation policy and key material; replacing the service without the original authorization material can require VM-owner action.
quick_check: What attack becomes easier if the same privileged identity can administer both HGS policy and every guarded Hyper-V host?

title: HGS Attestation Modes, Guarded Host Prerequisites and Authorization Evidence
summary: Compare TPM-trusted and host-key attestation, recognize deprecated admin-trusted mode, and evaluate the artifacts required to authorize guarded hosts safely.
objective: Select an attestation design from security requirements and hardware capability, and explain what evidence HGS evaluates before authorizing a host.
body_outline: TPM-trusted attestation provides the stronger trust model and uses TPM identity plus measured boot and code-integrity evidence to determine host health.
Host-key attestation is simpler and authorizes a host using a registered public host key; it is useful where TPM-trusted attestation requirements cannot be met.
Admin-trusted Active Directory attestation is deprecated beginning with Windows Server 2019 and should not be chosen as the target design for a new guarded fabric.
TPM mode requires compatible platform capabilities including TPM 2.0, UEFI and hardware virtualization protections documented by Microsoft.

Authorization artifacts must be lifecycle-managed when hardware, firmware or approved software baselines change; broadening policy simply to clear an attestation failure weakens the security boundary.
quick_check: Why is registering a host key not equivalent to proving the host booted a measured approved software configuration?

title: Shielded VM Key Release, HGS Certificates, Operations and Disaster Recovery
summary: Relate guarded-host attestation, HGS signing/encryption keys, shielded VM startup and HGS recovery into one operational security model.
architecture_notes: HGS attestation determines whether a host is trusted, while the key protection service controls release of the material required to unlock shielded workloads. HGS signing and encryption keys are therefore part of the workload availability and confidentiality boundary. Microsoft guidance treats HGS state, attestation policies and key material as items that must be deliberately backed up and restored; an ordinary full-system-image assumption is not the recommended HGS recovery model.
failure_modes: HGS signing or encryption private keys lost or compromised
all HGS nodes unavailable during a protected workload restart
attestation policy drift authorizes an unintended host or rejects a compliant host
TPM or code-integrity baseline changes without controlled policy lifecycle
DNS or service endpoint failure prevents a guarded host reaching HGS
disaster recovery rebuild uses new HGS keys that existing VM owners have not authorized
privileged-role overlap allows a fabric administrator to influence HGS trust decisions
enterprise_design_notes: Treat HGS like a security control plane: isolate administration, maintain resilient service endpoints, protect and escrow recovery material, monitor attestation policy changes, test recovery without weakening trust, and require explicit security approval for policy or key changes.

title: Read-Only HGS and Guarded Host Evidence Pack
summary: Collect HGS service, attestation, guarded-host and certificate metadata without changing trust mode, policy, keys or VM protection state.
objective: Create a timestamped evidence pack that can support HGS health, attestation and DR review before any guarded-fabric change is approved.
steps: Record HGS service configuration, attestation mode and published attestation/key-protection endpoints.
List currently configured attestation policies and trusted host-key or TPM authorization objects appropriate to the active mode.
From a guarded host, record HGS client configuration and whether the host reports as guarded without changing endpoints.
Capture HGS diagnostic output and recent relevant events when troubleshooting is required.
Inventory the presence, ownership, expiry and backup status of HGS signing/encryption certificate material without exporting private keys during routine evidence collection.
Document unresolved policy, endpoint, certificate, host-health or recovery-material gaps before authorizing a change.
expected_result: A read-only HGS/guarded-host evidence pack with no attestation-mode change, policy mutation, key export, host authorization or VM protection change.

title: HGS Attestation or Shielded VM Startup Incident Decision Tree
summary: Diagnose guarded-fabric failures by separating HGS availability, endpoint reachability, host attestation, certificate/key and VM authorization causes before changing trust policy.
diagnostic_order: Classify the incident as HGS service outage, endpoint/DNS/TLS failure, host attestation failure, key-protection failure or shielded-VM authorization failure.
Confirm HGS cluster/service health and the published attestation/key-protection URLs before touching host policy.
From the affected host, record HGS client configuration and detailed diagnostics; compare with a known-good guarded host.
For TPM mode, compare TPM identity, baseline and code-integrity evidence with currently enabled HGS policies; for host-key mode, verify the registered public key identity.
Check signing/encryption certificate availability, validity and protected key ownership without exporting or replacing private keys as a diagnostic shortcut.
Correlate policy, certificate, host firmware/software and HGS changes by time, then escalate with preserved evidence before any policy or trust mutation.
escalation_boundary: Do not switch attestation modes, disable/remove attestation policies, register replacement host identities, replace HGS signing/encryption keys, unshield a VM, or bypass HGS trust merely to restore service without approved security/change authority and a documented recovery path.

title: HGS and Shielded VM Foundations Assessment
summary: Scenario assessment covering trust boundaries, attestation modes, key protection, HGS recovery and safe troubleshooting decisions.

assessment_items.question: Why is admin-trusted Active Directory attestation a poor target for a new guarded fabric?
assessment_items.answer: Microsoft deprecates AD mode beginning with Windows Server 2019; TPM-trusted attestation provides stronger measured trust, while host-key attestation is the supported simpler alternative when TPM mode is not feasible.

assessment_items.question: What does TPM-trusted attestation prove that host-key attestation does not?
assessment_items.answer: It can evaluate platform identity plus measured boot and code-integrity evidence rather than only possession of an authorized host key.

assessment_items.question: Why must HGS signing and encryption keys be included in DR planning?
assessment_items.answer: They participate in authorization and key release for shielded VMs; losing the original protected key material can force workload owners to authorize replacement keys before protected VMs can run.

assessment_items.question: A host stops attesting after firmware maintenance. What is the unsafe shortcut?
assessment_items.answer: Broadening or disabling attestation policy until the host passes. The correct response is to preserve diagnostics and determine whether the changed measured state is expected, approved and safe before modifying policy.

title: Senior HGS Interview: Guarded Fabric Architecture, Attestation and Recovery
summary: Senior production scenarios testing HGS trust design, attestation troubleshooting, privileged-role separation and disaster-recovery reasoning.

questions.question: Design an HGS trust boundary for a production Hyper-V estate. What must be separated or independently protected?
answer_points: HGS administration from fabric administration
HGS directory/forest trust boundary
signing and encryption private keys
attestation policy authority
DNS/service endpoint availability
backup and DR custody
auditing of policy and privileged changes

questions.question: A newly patched guarded host fails TPM attestation while peer hosts succeed. What is your evidence-first sequence?
answer_points: run detailed HGS diagnostics
compare TPM/platform identifier
compare measured baseline and CI policy
review firmware/software change evidence
confirm HGS policy state and mode
do not disable policy to make the host pass
approve a new baseline only after security validation

questions.question: When would host-key attestation be chosen instead of TPM-trusted attestation?
answer_points: hardware or operational constraints prevent TPM mode
organization accepts the weaker assurance model
host public keys can be securely registered and lifecycle-managed
risk decision is documented
AD-trusted mode is not selected as the new target merely for convenience

questions.question: All HGS nodes and backups are lost, but shielded VM disks survive. Why may ordinary Hyper-V recovery still fail?
answer_points: shielded VM key release depends on an authorized guardian/HGS trust
replacement HGS signing/encryption keys differ
existing VM owners may need to authorize new keys
attestation policy and host authorization evidence must be rebuilt
this is why HGS state and keys need tested independent recovery
